column1: 1|system|Turn the questions into a design brief|For a new gate or production machine, define the movement before selecting the power unit: required force or torque, travel, cycle time and what must happen when power is lost. Separate the peak demand from the normal duty so the supplier can assess both capacity and control.|Record a commissioning baseline for cycle time, pressure and water condition. Those measurements give maintenance staff a reference when movement becomes slower or less consistent.

2|cylinder|Use area before raising pressure|A larger piston area can meet a higher load at the available pressure, but it also increases stroke volume. Check the required cycle time and return flow before enlarging the cylinder; a force improvement can otherwise create a valve or pipework restriction.|Trend loaded extension and retraction separately. Increasing a relief setting to compensate for wear can exceed a weaker component's limit without correcting the underlying loss.

3|system|Compare the same completed movement|Compare air and water on the same actuator duty, including holding time and control accuracy. Assess electrical input at the supply equipment, not only actuator output; unloaded operation, leakage and standby can change the annual result.|Include inspection of distribution leaks and the cost of maintaining the shared utility. Allocate only the portion attributable to the proposed machine when comparing lifecycle costs.

4|environment|Measure the boundary of the improvement|For a municipal gate conversion, identify the oil inventory removed and the electricity and water that the replacement consumes. Keep those measurements distinct from wider corporate ESG indicators so the project benefit can be traced to a specific asset.|Retain meter readings, service records and replacement-part quantities. Update the environmental comparison after an operating season rather than carrying the original forecast forward unchanged.

5|specification|Match documents to the supplied assembly|For marine or food applications, list which parts contact process water, which face washdown and which carry structural loads. Request evidence for the exact offered model, materials and service; a certificate for a material does not establish approval of the assembled system.|Keep document revisions with the equipment serial record. Review replacement seals, coatings and fittings against the approved configuration before purchasing substitutes.

6|environment|Prioritise the actual release pathway|Map a credible leak from its source to the drain, waterway or process. Compare eliminating the working-oil inventory with improving containment, using the same operating function. This makes the equipment decision specific enough to price and maintain.|Track incidents and near misses without turning an assumed event probability into a measured fact. Revisit the cost comparison when the operating location or drainage arrangement changes.

7|system|Specify motion as well as force|A hatch or gate needs a defined acceleration, travel speed, stopping behaviour and holding state. Size the actuator for load, then check whether the pump and control valve can deliver that movement across the expected pressure range.|Record command, position and pressure together during acceptance. Repeating the same loaded cycle later helps distinguish mechanical binding from hydraulic loss or a feedback fault.

8|economics|Build the investment case from service records|Separate purchase and installation cost from recurring energy, filters, labour and planned replacement. Compare a water proposal with a credible alternative that delivers the same service, then test what happens if operating hours or savings are lower than expected.|Include major service events in the year they are expected to occur. Avoid counting the same avoided outage both as an operating saving and as a separate risk benefit.

9|accumulator|Size the movement after power loss|Define the load and travel needed for the safe state, then identify the energy source that remains available. If a gas accumulator is proposed, assess usable volume between the actual maximum and minimum operating pressures, not its shell volume alone.|Include periodic verification of stored-energy availability and controlled recovery after a trip. A manual override must be accessible and must not unexpectedly release a suspended or restrained load.

10|retrofit|Separate reusable machinery from fluid components|A retrofit survey should distinguish the machine frame and linkage from pumps, valves, hoses, seals and sliding interfaces. Record each retained component's water-service evidence; the presence of a stainless housing alone is insufficient.|Plan flushing, temporary isolation, spare parts and recommissioning within the outage. Compare the full conversion cost with replacement before ordering an apparently simple fluid change.

11|winter|Protect the least visible trapped volume|For an outdoor unit, examine dead legs, valve cavities and instrument lines as well as the reservoir. State the coldest storage and shutdown conditions, and decide whether the supported strategy is heating, enclosure or drain-down.|Verify protection before seasonal shutdown and after a power interruption. Include heater electricity, inspections and restart checks in the operating budget rather than treating freeze protection as a one-time purchase.

12|cylinder|Check both directions under load|For a lifting or pushing mechanism, use the cap-end and annular areas separately. Opposing chamber pressure reduces net force; the rod also changes the required flow and speed on retraction. Check the weakest linkage position through the stroke.|Measure load-related drift and stroke time under repeatable conditions. A cylinder with adequate static force can still require service because of leakage, damaged guidance or mechanical misalignment.

13|materials|Specify the complete sliding pair|For a bearing or guide, identify the polymer grade, counterface material, finish, contact load and movement. Carbon reinforcement is part of the material description; it does not establish an allowable speed or service life for every geometry.|Retain the original wear dimensions and replacement criteria. Investigate abrasive contamination and alignment when wear changes, rather than attributing all degradation to the polymer choice.

14|suction|Start at the pump inlet|For a long suction line, account for source level, temperature, fittings and filter restriction under the highest required flow. Compare available inlet conditions with the pump supplier's requirements; a discharge-pressure setting cannot demonstrate a satisfactory inlet.|Record inlet pressure alongside flow and noise at commissioning. Recheck when filters load, source level falls or water warms, because the same pump can encounter different inlet conditions through the year.

15|cylinder|Select the cylinder and its mounting together|For a gate linkage, calculate force at the actual attachment points through the full stroke. Choose bore and rod dimensions with available chamber pressures, then review buckling, side load and removal clearance with the mounting arrangement.|Provide a way to inspect rod surfaces and pins without dismantling the entire gate. Budget for access and alignment checks as well as seal replacement.

16|marine|Separate internal water from coastal exposure|A deck mechanism may use controlled freshwater internally while its rod and fittings face salt spray. Describe both environments when selecting the cylinder, valves and power unit; the word marine does not define the fluid chemistry.|Plan drainage, exterior rinsing where specified, and inspection of crevices and dissimilar-metal connections. Include preservation during lay-up in the vessel's maintenance schedule.

17|maintenance|Replace the oil task list with a water task list|Removing oil changes fluid handling, but filters, seals, hoses, corrosion control and monitoring still require attention. Build the service plan from the water circuit and duty rather than deleting the former oil-maintenance schedule wholesale.|Record labour, consumables and downtime separately during the first service interval. That evidence supports a fair lifecycle comparison and helps refine the next interval.

18|motor|Treat the air motor as a separate drive choice|If an air motor drives a water pump, match its speed and torque curve to the pump's demand and coupling. Compressed-air supply pressure and consumption belong in the drive assessment; the water motor calculator does not predict air-motor performance.|Inspect the coupling and both utility supplies. Account for compressor energy and air-system servicing when comparing the complete arrangement with an electric drive.

19|ro|Separate process pumping from utility actuation|Distinguish the RO high-pressure feed duty from cylinders or valves that operate plant equipment. Specify feed salinity, temperature, permeate target and recovery for the process equipment, then assess any hydraulic actuator circuit independently.|Trend process flow, pressure and water quality together. A rise in pressure may reflect membrane or pretreatment conditions, so investigate the process before changing the pump selection.

20|hpu|Size a power unit around simultaneous demand|List which actuators move together and for how long. Add concurrent flows, assess the governing pressure and account for return flow; summing every actuator's peak demand can oversize a unit that operates sequentially.|Measure standby draw as well as active input. Include reservoir access, filter changes and removal space in the layout so routine servicing remains practical after installation.

21|valve|Match metering behaviour to the load|Select a valve for the required flow at the available pressure difference, including low-speed operation. A valve that passes peak flow may still give poor control near closure; use the supplier's water-service characteristic and leakage information.|Trend command, movement and pressure together. Check contamination and the mechanical load before adjusting control parameters to compensate for sticking or inconsistent travel.

22|system|Define what closed loop means in the schematic|Identify whether the term describes a recirculating fluid path, feedback control or both. Draw replenishment, cooling, pressure protection and return routes explicitly so each operating state has an understood pressure balance.|Monitor water condition and temperature at consistent locations. Include losses during holding and recirculation in the annual energy estimate, not only the useful actuator stroke.

23|system|Design the return path with the supply path|For a multi-actuator circuit, trace return flows during extension, retraction and simultaneous motion. Return restriction creates opposing pressure and can change both force and speed even when pump supply pressure is adequate.|Provide accessible pressure measurement points before commissioning. Their small installation cost can reduce later troubleshooting time and unnecessary component replacement.

24|cylinder|Locate the loss before changing the cylinder|Measure pressure at the power unit and both cylinder chambers during the problematic movement. Compare unloaded and loaded travel; the difference helps separate line losses, opposing pressure and mechanical resistance.|Record valve position, water temperature and flow with each test. Replacing a seal or raising pressure without that context can leave a restricted return line unresolved.

25|filtration|Specify water quality and filtration separately|Particle filtration does not remove dissolved salts or necessarily control microorganisms. Give the supplier a water analysis and the operating temperature, then select filter media, rating and location for the equipment's actual requirement.|Trend filter differential pressure and inspect retained debris. Rising restriction or unusual deposits should trigger investigation of the source and circuit, not an automatic change to a coarser filter.

26|ro|Design for the source-water range|Seasonal salinity and temperature can change the RO operating duty. Establish the feed range and production requirement before comparing power centres, and check pretreatment and storage alongside high-pressure pumping.|Use operating data from low-demand and peak-demand periods. Include membrane cleaning, pretreatment consumables and downtime in the lifecycle assessment so pump energy is not mistaken for total plant cost.

27|spray|Match the spray to the dust source|Define the dust source, capture zone and available water quality, then select the nozzle arrangement and required pressure. An orifice estimate can check a flow assumption, but it cannot predict droplet distribution or dust-capture performance.|Record nozzle pressure and inspect for wear or blockage. A changed spray pattern can increase water use or reduce capture even while the pump continues to run normally.

28|pump|Compare efficiency at matched duty points|Compare pumps at the same delivered flow, pressure difference, speed and water condition. Separate volumetric loss from torque-related loss; a single peak-efficiency figure does not describe operation over an intermittent duty cycle.|Repeat measurements with calibrated flow, pressure and drive data. Use trends to schedule investigation before higher leakage or friction becomes a production interruption.

29|system|Compare the complete actuator installation|For a remote gate, include electric supply, controls, mechanical transmission and service access in both options. Compare holding and power-loss behaviour as well as travel force; those requirements can change the preferred equipment arrangement.|Estimate replacement access and expected outage duration for each option. Use a common study period and residual-value basis instead of comparing purchase prices alone.

30|energy|Measure the whole operating cycle|Separate starting, loaded travel, holding and idle periods when estimating annual input. Pressure multiplied by flow gives hydraulic output; electrical input also reflects pump, drive and control losses at each state.|Log input power and operating hours after commissioning. Recalculate the forecast if the machine spends more time idle or bypassing flow than the design assumed.

31|system|Connect pressure, flow and useful work|Start with the mechanism's load and speed, translate them into actuator pressure and flow, then add circuit losses. This order helps avoid selecting a large power unit before the useful movement is defined.|Keep the original design duty with the asset record. Later changes to cycle time or loading should trigger a system review rather than an isolated pressure adjustment.

32|seals|Use geometry as one part of seal selection|An O-ring squeeze calculation checks dimensions; it does not establish dynamic friction, extrusion resistance or fluid compatibility. Supply pressure, temperature, speed, surface condition and water chemistry when requesting the seal arrangement.|Record the failure location and appearance when seals are removed. Repeated damage at the same position can point to misalignment or surface damage that a new seal alone will not correct.

33|environment|Translate the environmental objective into equipment scope|Identify the circuit, oil inventory and release pathways affected by the proposal. Specify the operating function and evidence needed for the project so a water conversion can be evaluated alongside containment and maintenance improvements.|Maintain a record of water discharge, service waste and energy use after conversion. Removing working oil changes the risk profile but does not remove every environmental management task.

34|specification|Keep the technical brief usable as requirements change|State the installation location, process exposure and required operating function before requesting equipment. Record who will verify applicable requirements and which documents must accompany the supplied assembly.|Keep a revision history for the requirement register. A later process or site change may require reassessment even when the hydraulic hardware remains unchanged.

35|environment|Rank the vulnerable assets first|A cylinder over an open channel has a different release pathway from an enclosed machine with drainage containment. Rank assets by exposure, operating importance and conversion feasibility, then develop a defined equipment duty for the strongest candidate.|Use inspection and incident records to update the ranking. Include access and downtime in the lifecycle estimate so the first conversion is practical to support.

36|safety|Define and verify the safety function separately|For attraction equipment, specify the required response to power loss, a hose fault or an invalid sensor signal. Select the actuator and valves within the system safety design; fluid choice alone does not establish a safe stopping or holding function.|Keep proof-test procedures and restoration checks with the asset. Service changes that affect valve behaviour, stored energy or feedback need review before the equipment returns to operation.

37|fire|Start with the fire hazard and approved arrangement|Choose water-mist equipment from the required hazard coverage and supported nozzle-system combination. Pressure and flow calculations help assess supply demand but do not establish fire suppression effectiveness or approval of a new nozzle layout.|Track pump condition, nozzle obstruction and water-supply availability through the specified inspection programme. Include the operational impact of testing and planned outages in the ownership assessment.

38|marine|Use a vessel concept as a design exercise|For a hydrogen-vessel concept, separate propulsion and fuel-system requirements from hydraulic deck functions. Define a specific hatch, ramp or winch duty before considering water components, without treating the concept as verified fleet performance.|Evaluate crew access, spare parts and lay-up preservation for the proposed circuit. Keep expected benefits labelled as design estimates until operating measurements are available.

39|valve|Choose actuation from the process-valve load|Obtain the valve manufacturer's thrust or torque requirement across the operating range, including breakaway and seating. Match the actuator and hydraulic control to that envelope rather than sizing from nominal pipe diameter.|Record stroke time and the pressure trace during acceptance. Changes in seating demand can reveal process deposits or mechanical wear before a failed operation.

40|fluid|Use properties at the actual operating temperature|Density and viscosity affect velocity, friction and leakage assumptions. Use the working fluid's condition in line-loss calculations, and keep those calculations separate from the pump or valve manufacturer's permitted operating envelope.|Track temperature with performance measurements. Comparing a warm operating test with a cold commissioning baseline can misidentify a property change as equipment deterioration.

41|maintenance|Define what clean start-up means|A flushing plan needs a target, sampling location and completion criterion appropriate to the supplied components. Protect sensitive valves and seals during the procedure and confirm the final circuit arrangement before operation.|Keep flushing results and initial filter inspections in the service record. Early debris observations can identify assembly contamination before it becomes repeated valve or seal damage.

42|industrial|Select one industrial movement at a time|For a sawmill clamp or steel-mill gate, document load, heat exposure, contamination and cycle frequency. Distinguish hydraulic actuation from process-water spraying so the pump and controls are selected for the intended function.|Plan maintenance around production access and isolation. Include hose routing, inspection clearance and spare-component availability when comparing installation options.

43|economics|Establish viability before assuming funding|Prepare the equipment scope and operating-cost case without a grant, then examine a separate funded scenario using confirmed project information. This shows which design decisions depend on support and which remain worthwhile on operating merit.|Keep quotations, baseline measurements and project records organised from the start. Review forecast savings against measured operation after commissioning rather than treating awarded support as proof of technical performance.

44|pump|Check the smallest useful flow as well as the largest|A positioning circuit may spend much of its time below peak demand. Check the pump-control arrangement and valve behaviour at that low flow, then assess how the system supplies occasional fast movement without excessive bypass loss.|Record low-speed stability and standby power during acceptance. Those measurements reveal costs and control limitations that a maximum-flow demonstration can miss.

45|specification|Make the fluid boundary explicit in the specification|State which circuit must use water and which external lubricated mechanisms may remain. Identify the water source, temperature, load, motion and required documentation so suppliers can offer a defined assembly rather than a broad oil-free claim.|Require service instructions and a supported spare-parts list with the proposal. Include the cost of routine inspection and planned replacement in the tender comparison.

46|cylinder|Calculate net force at the chambers|For a double-acting cylinder, account for supply pressure acting on one effective area and return pressure acting on the opposing area. Check extension and retraction independently before applying the project's load and mechanical allowances.|Measure both chamber pressures when investigating weak motion. Pump outlet pressure alone can hide an obstructed return or a loss between the power unit and cylinder.

47|fluid|Include trapped-fluid heating in the design review|A blocked-in section can experience pressure change as temperature rises even without pump operation. Identify isolated volumes, solar exposure and process heat when reviewing the circuit and its pressure-protection arrangement.|Inspect thermal protection and isolation procedures during planned service. Record the operating temperature with leak or drift observations so the cause can be assessed in context.

48|economics|Separate predictable service from uncertain events|Use invoices and maintenance logs for recurring costs, and model spills or outages as separate scenarios. Compare both options over the same working life and avoid presenting a rare-event assumption as an annual saving already achieved.|Update the model with actual labour, consumables and energy after installation. Keep unusually costly incidents visible instead of hiding them inside an unexplained average.

49|wastewater|Find the machinery-to-process connection|Map where hydraulic leakage could enter a channel, tank or sludge stream. Develop the replacement actuator duty at that location, including debris loading, isolation needs and access, before selecting a water power unit.|Record service work and any process interruptions separately. A reduction in hydraulic-oil exposure is useful, but treatment performance still needs its own operating evidence.

50|hpu|Make the HPU match the production schedule|For an intermittent industrial duty, distinguish short movement peaks from long holding periods. Specify simultaneous operation, restart behaviour and utility availability so the power unit can be sized around the real sequence.|Meter input during an entire production shift, including idle time. Compare measured standby and active consumption with the proposal before attributing savings to the working fluid alone.

51|economics|Keep the equipment decision independent of an assumed credit|Build an unsubsidised cost comparison first, then use a separate scenario for any confirmed incentive. Identify the qualifying equipment and project costs through the appropriate current review rather than applying a percentage to the whole installation.|Retain dated quotations and actual commissioning costs. Revisit the financial model if the eligible scope or implementation schedule changes.

52|retrofit|Convert the circuit as an engineered assembly|Inventory every wetted component and its materials, clearances, seals and service history. Retaining the frame or prime mover may be practical, but the suitability of an oil-service pump or valve cannot be inferred from the machine's previous performance.|Plan removal of residual oil and contamination, verification of the new water circuit, and operator training. Include those activities in the outage and lifecycle budgets.

53|winter|Turn winterisation into a repeatable procedure|Identify the water that remains in cylinders, valves and low points after draining. Define which components stay heated, which can be emptied and which require supplier-approved preservation, including during loss of normal power.|Use a pre-winter inspection and a documented restart check. Include inspection labour and heat-tracing energy when comparing enclosed and exposed installations.

54|environment|Define the oil source removed by the conversion|A water working circuit removes its own hydraulic-oil inventory; gearboxes or other lubricated mechanisms may still exist nearby. Mark the scope on the equipment drawing so the environmental benefit is precise and auditable.|Inspect remaining lubricated equipment and manage water releases appropriately. Keep the service comparison focused on the tasks actually changed by the conversion.

55|system|Translate a familiar oil duty into water requirements|Retain the useful load and movement requirements, then reassess the components and losses for water. Pressure and area still determine ideal force, while the pump, seals and sliding interfaces must support the chosen fluid.|Establish a new commissioning baseline after conversion. Historic oil-system pressure settings and maintenance intervals should not automatically become the water-system operating standard.

56|pump|Locate the losses behind the efficiency claim|Separate leakage, mechanical friction, line losses and control losses when evaluating a water pump circuit. Equipment designed for water can address these mechanisms, but an additive-free fluid does not itself establish total system efficiency.|Measure delivered flow, pressure and input power at representative operating points. Use the same boundaries when comparing new measurements with the original selection.

57|environment|Follow all contamination pathways|For equipment near food or process water, distinguish hydraulic-oil removal from sanitary design, source-water quality and cross-connections. Define the actual contact or release pathway before selecting the actuator and its water supply.|Include backflow protection, water management and cleaning procedures in the maintenance review where applicable. Track these tasks alongside the oil-handling work that has been removed.

58|economics|Use one technical baseline for different funding scenarios|Define the equipment duty, baseline operating costs and measurable project outcomes once. Assess each potential funding route against that documented scope, keeping unconfirmed assistance out of the base investment case.|Retain engineering decisions, trial observations and cost records as the project progresses. Reconcile the forecast with actual operating data after commissioning.

59|gate|Size for the governing gate condition|Obtain gate thrust across the full travel and relevant water-level conditions, including seating and breakaway. Check mounting geometry and opposing hydraulic pressure before choosing cylinder size and power-unit flow.|Provide safe access for pin, seal and position-feedback inspection. Test the required movement under agreed conditions and record the results for later seasonal comparison.

60|system|Keep power and energy distinct|Power describes the rate of useful work during movement; energy includes how long each operating state lasts. Calculate the required pressure and flow at the load, then include losses and operating hours when selecting the drive.|Record both peak demand and accumulated energy. A unit that meets peak output may still have avoidable annual cost if it runs continuously through long idle periods.

61|gate|Assess the gate, waterway and actuator together|For an intake or isolation gate, hydraulic load changes with water level and gate position. Use the gate supplier's load envelope and the structural mounting design, then verify the required opening, closing and holding functions.|Include infrequent-operation checks and access during high-water conditions in the service plan. Long standby makes first-movement evidence particularly valuable.

62|environment|Prioritise exposure rather than applying a blanket rule|Start with machinery over open water, near product contact or beside vulnerable drainage. Evaluate water actuation against its required load, control and service conditions so the environmental objective produces a workable equipment proposal.|Compare both the removed oil tasks and the added water-management tasks. Use those records to select subsequent conversion candidates.

63|economics|Test the cost drivers that can reverse the result|Compare energy, routine labour, consumables and major replacement under the expected operating schedule. Run low- and high-utilisation scenarios rather than assuming every site benefits from the same fluid-service reduction.|Update maintenance frequency and outage estimates as operating evidence accumulates. Keep the study period and discount assumptions consistent between alternatives.

64|fluid|Treat viscosity as a design input|Lower viscosity changes leakage and lubrication behaviour, so component clearances and sliding pairs matter. Use viscosity at the intended water temperature for line calculations and obtain the supplier's operating envelope for the pump and valve assembly.|Trend flow and input power as temperature changes. A pressure reading alone will not reveal how much flow is being lost internally.

65|thermal|Account for heat even when temperature appears stable|A circuit may reject heat quickly enough to show little bulk temperature rise while still consuming energy through throttling and leakage. Estimate losses from pressure and flow, then assess how heat leaves the actual installation.|Record temperatures at consistent locations with electrical input and duty. Include cooling equipment and standby operation in the energy comparison where they are part of the system.

66|gate|Use the knife-gate manufacturer's thrust data|Seating, unseating and travel through process material can govern different loads. Match the water cylinder to the full thrust envelope and installation geometry, then check closing time and the pressure available at the actuator.|Trend stroke time and seating pressure. Increased demand may indicate deposits or guide wear in the process valve rather than a shortage of hydraulic capacity.

67|economics|Place replacements in the correct year|A lifecycle model should distinguish annual service from a future pump, seal or power-unit replacement. Apply the same study period and residual-value treatment to both options so timing does not distort the comparison.|Keep actual replacement dates and costs in the asset record. Use them to refine the next investment decision instead of reusing a generic percentage of capital cost.

68|industrial|Review the load path in forestry equipment|For a clamp or hauling mechanism, distinguish the hydraulic duty from structural stability and load restraint. Describe shock loading, contamination, hose movement and cold exposure before selecting a cylinder or motor circuit.|Plan inspection of exposed hoses, mountings and rod surfaces around field access. Account for travel time and downtime when comparing service costs with workshop-based equipment.

69|seals|Make seal-life evidence specific to the duty|Record stroke, speed, pressure, dwell time and water condition when discussing expected service. A calendar interval from a lightly used installation does not directly predict performance in a continuously cycling machine.|Trend leakage and friction-related behaviour before failure. On removal, inspect the counterface and guides so replacement addresses the cause as well as the worn seal.

70|materials|Specify chemistry and contact together|Assess the wetted metals, polymer grade and sliding counterface as an assembly. State chloride exposure, temperature, deposits and electrical contact between dissimilar metals; naming 316 stainless and PEEK alone leaves important design conditions undefined.|Inspect crevices, deposits and wear interfaces during service. Preserve the supplied material pairing when ordering replacement parts unless a reviewed alternative is provided.

71|materials|Evaluate the counterface before choosing a polymer|Contact pressure, sliding speed, roughness and water condition act together at the interface. Request evidence for the proposed pair under the relevant duty rather than transferring a wear claim from an unrelated test.|Record surface condition and wear dimensions at repeatable locations. A roughened or damaged metal counterface can undermine a replacement polymer part even when its grade is unchanged.

72|industrial|Select for the mine environment and the movement|Define the specific gate, clamp or auxiliary drive duty, including dust, washdown, water quality and installation access. Separate the hydraulic power demand from any process-water service sharing the same site.|Include contamination control and remote access in the maintenance plan. Compare availability using planned service and measured failures rather than assuming fluid choice guarantees lower downtime.

73|gate|Turn the municipal objective into an asset plan|Choose a gate or valve with a defined oil-exposure pathway, then document its thrust, travel, frequency and fault response. This gives procurement a complete water-actuation scope that can be compared with maintaining the existing installation.|Include inspection access, spares and staff training in the ownership plan. Review performance after the first representative operating season before extending the approach to other assets.

74|environment|Count the benefit and the remaining flows|Identify the working oil removed, then account separately for electricity, water use and service materials. A recirculating system and a once-through arrangement have different water-management implications that belong in the comparison.|Use actual replenishment and service records after commissioning. Keep remaining lubricants and waste streams visible so the environmental statement matches the supplied installation.

75|safety|Give the pilot measurable acceptance criteria|For attraction equipment, define the trial load, movement, control response and fault tests before selecting hardware. Treat observations as evidence for that tested configuration, not automatic proof for a different ride or safety function.|Retain the test conditions, deviations and service findings. Use them to decide what further validation and maintenance provisions are needed before wider application.

76|environment|Connect environmental goals to measured work|Define the circuit boundary and useful output before estimating energy or emissions changes. Separate the direct removal of working oil from any calculated electricity-related benefit, which depends on the actual energy difference and emission factor.|Retain the factors, dates and measurements behind the comparison. Update the estimate when operating hours, electricity supply or replacement scope changes.

77|system|Compare complete circuits under the same duty|Use the same load, speed, holding time and annual schedule for water and oil options. Include pumps, valves, filtration, cooling and service access so the comparison does not favour one fluid by omitting its supporting equipment.|Measure energy and maintenance against the same boundary after commissioning. Keep assumptions about downtime and spill events separate from observed recurring costs.

78|system|Compare operation, installation and ownership together|For a replacement power unit, assess the whole installation from utility connection to actuator return. Check the minimum controlled movement and fault state as well as peak force, then price installation and routine service on that basis.|Maintain a common asset log for energy, labour, consumables and interruptions. That makes the long-term comparison more useful than a single catalogue efficiency figure.

79|valve|Test severe-service actuation against a defined load|Obtain the process valve's thrust or torque envelope, including deposits, seating and breakaway. Specify the hydraulic control and actuator response needed to reproduce that duty in a representative test.|Record cycle count, water condition, pressure traces and inspection findings. Treat the outcome as evidence for the tested configuration and preserve those conditions in the service plan.

80|pressure|Find the weakest rated element and the highest transient|Compare the pressure limits of the pump, valves, cylinder, hoses and fittings at the operating temperature. Then assess transient and trapped-fluid conditions; the normal pump setting is only one part of the pressure envelope.|Keep settings and component ratings with the schematic. After maintenance, verify that substituted parts and relief adjustments remain compatible with the complete circuit.

81|materials|Trace the corrosion mechanism|For wetted dissimilar metals, electrical contact and an electrolyte can create galvanic corrosion. Also consider crevices, deposits and water chemistry; changing the main housing material does not resolve every vulnerable joint or internal component.|Inspect fasteners, connections and stagnant locations as well as open surfaces. Record where attack occurs so the corrective action addresses the mechanism rather than only replacing the damaged part.

82|materials|Design out vulnerable details where possible|Review material compatibility, crevices, drainage and stagnant water before relying on a coating or chemical treatment. State the actual water chemistry and external exposure when asking the supplier to select the assembly.|Track deposits and local attack during inspection. Cleaning and preservation remain relevant even where the selected construction reduces dependence on protective coatings.

83|filtration|Distinguish particles from dissolved scale precursors|A particle filter can capture solids but does not remove dissolved hardness. Identify the deposit, water source and temperature before changing filtration or treatment, and check compatibility with the supplied components.|Trend restriction and inspect deposits at repeatable intervals. Include cleaning access and approved cleaning methods in the design so maintenance does not require improvised chemicals.

84|retrofit|Build the steel-mill retrofit around the outage|Document the mechanism's load, radiant heat, contamination and operating sequence before replacing its hydraulic circuit. Confirm which structural and drive components can be retained and which wetted parts require water-specific selection.|Plan isolation, removal, flushing, installation and loaded recommissioning as separate tasks. Include contingency time and critical spares rather than assuming a fluid conversion fits an ordinary service stop.

85|fire|Preserve the required fire-water function through the retrofit|Establish the required supply duty and approved system arrangement before selecting a replacement pump. Assess controls, power supply, suction conditions and testing provisions together so a pump change does not leave an unsupported system configuration.|Plan the outage and restoration test with the responsible site team. Include routine testing and water-supply checks in ownership cost, not only pump servicing.

86|seals|Specify the hose assembly as well as the elastomer|Water compatibility of the inner tube is only one selection item. Check pressure, temperature, end fittings, bend radius, movement and external exposure for the complete hose assembly.|Inspect for abrasion, fitting damage and changes in flexibility using the supplier's criteria. Record service history and replace based on the supported maintenance plan rather than a universal lifetime claim.

87|pump|Select from the required delivered flow|Establish flow at the actuator or process, add relevant leakage and circuit demand, then evaluate pump displacement and speed. Check inlet conditions, drive torque and the supplied water-service configuration before comparing model sizes.|Record flow, pressure and input at commissioning. Declining output at the same speed warrants investigation of inlet supply, leakage and wear before increasing drive speed.

88|maintenance|Make the outage estimate task-based|List isolation, depressurisation, draining, access, component work, flushing and restart verification separately. Check which spare parts and lifting arrangements must be available before shutdown; a short hands-on repair does not define the complete outage.|Capture actual task times during service. Use that evidence to improve the next outage plan and the lifecycle estimate without promising the same duration at every installation.

89|specification|Ask bidders to demonstrate the required duty|Describe load, travel, timing, water condition, environment and fault response in the tender. Request the offered equipment configuration and supporting data so water and alternative proposals can be assessed against the same requirement.|Evaluate service access, spares and replacement procedures with purchase cost. An incomplete maintenance scope can make a low initial price expensive to operate.

90|cylinder|Size flow after choosing effective area|Once force establishes a candidate bore and rod, calculate stroke volume and the flow needed for the required time in each direction.
